text: Aggregation means combining produce from several smallholder farms so farmers can approach buyers with a larger, more consistent quantity — particularly relevant in Preah Vihear given cassava, cashew, soybean, and rice production and a national average holding of about 1.7 hectares (nearly 44% below 1 hectare). Aggregation can make it easier to negotiate with a rice mill, trader, processor, or larger buyer that would not find it economical to collect a small quantity from one farm, and can reduce per-unit transport/handling cost. However, aggregation does not automatically mean a higher price — if poor-quality produce from one farm is mixed with good-quality produce from another, the buyer may downgrade or reject the whole lot. Farmers need agreed quality standards, individual weighing/records, and clear rules about who bears the loss when produce is downgraded. Fresh cassava roots need aggregation organized around harvesting and rapid delivery (they deteriorate quickly), while properly dried rice or cashew offer more flexibility for storage-based aggregation. During the wet season (roughly May–October), aggregation plans need to account for drying and temporary storage, since roads and moisture complicate collection; during the dry season (roughly November–April), collection is often easier but water and heat constraints remain. Informal aggregation among neighboring farmers is often more realistic than assuming a formal cooperative exists. The objective is larger, traceable, consistently graded lots — not simply the biggest possible combined pile.
